documents: Ezpeleta et al. 2022, Basin Research 34:1983-2012, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: However, the thermal effects of flat subduction onto a continental margin that underwent Mesozoic lithospheric stretching remain to be disentangled.

sequences.source_document: Ezpeleta et al. 2022, Basin Research (published PDF)

steps.action: Pose the unresolved question of how Mesozoic rifting and Miocene flat-slab subduction shaped the thermal history of the Ischigualasto-Villa Unión basin, where thermal studies are scarce.
steps.quote: the thermal effects of flat subduction onto a continental margin that underwent Mesozoic lithospheric stretching remain to be disentangled

steps.action: Take from other groups' work on the Cuyana Basin the model that the thermal maximum of the Triassic rift basins came from Cenozoic foreland burial.
steps.quote: it has been argued that the thermal maximum was triggered and controlled by the development of a Cenozoic foreland infilling

steps.action: State the rival: low Cenozoic gradients may have prevented burial-driven heating, so the peak temperatures could date from a Mesozoic high heat-flow regime.
steps.quote: An alternative hypothesis is that these temperatures could have been achieved during the Mesozoic, associated with a high heat flow regime.

steps.action: Design a multi-proxy study of three stratigraphic sections: vitrinite reflectance, XRD of clays, AFT, AHe and ZHe, and QTqt inverse modelling aimed at dating the thermal peak.
steps.quote: with a particular focus in documenting the age of the thermal peak and the time–temperature conditions attained during Cenozoic burial

steps.action: Measure %Ro in 29 samples and I/S ordering and illite content in 71 samples; find an abrupt jump in illite content across the Triassic–Cretaceous/Cenozoic contact and lower values in the eastern section.
steps.quote: an abrupt change from<5 to 65 illite% between the Cerro Rajado and Los Colorados Formations

steps.action: Obtain new AFT (9 samples), AHe (22 aliquots) and ZHe (2 aliquots) ages and pool them with published ages from Fosdick et al. (2015) and Ortíz et al. (2015).
steps.quote: we integrate our new data with 2 published AFT, 2 AHe and 1 ZHe ages

steps.action: Check whether age dispersion reflects annealing kinetics (Dpar) or radiation damage and grain size (eU, ESR); find no Dpar correlation and partial eU or size control.
steps.quote: but they are not characterized by the Dpar, as there is no correlation of ages with Dpar values

steps.action: Compare the young, reset AHe and AFT ages with independently published ages from the same section and find them concordant.
steps.quote: These young and reproducible AHe ages in the southern section are compatible with the ages obtained in one Triassic

steps.action: Invert four individual samples in QTqt with geological constraints: Mesozoic peak (~160°C, 210–150 Ma), weaker Cenozoic peak of 70–85°C, and cooling onset 15–4 Ma.
steps.quote: the obtained thermal histories suggest that the thermal peak was attained during Mesozoic times

steps.action: Because individual models disagree on the timing of Cenozoic cooling, run multi-sample models of the northern and southern profiles without a Triassic constraint.
steps.quote: In order to overcome this shortcoming, we conducted multi-sample thermal modelling.

steps.action: Find that the unconstrained models fit the data but give incompatible peak ages (~255 vs ~110 Ma) and Cenozoic temperatures for sites 35 km apart, and judge them unreliable.
steps.quote: these unconstrained models hardly represent a reliable history

steps.action: Rerun the multi-sample models with an added constraint of residence at up to 200°C at 210–180 Ma, motivated by the individual models, Triassic basalts and regional studies.
steps.quote: a second set of multi-sample models employed an additional constraint of residence at up to 200°C in the latest Triassic–earliest Jurassic

steps.action: Compare fits: the constrained model improves the log-likelihood in the south (−446 vs −994), is similar in the north, and gives final cooling at 7–9 Ma and a decreasing Cenozoic gradient.
steps.quote: significantly improve the model fit with respect to the observed data in the southern profile

steps.action: Convert %Ro and illite-in-I/S values into maximum temperatures per unit (110–140°C for Ischichuca–Los Rastros, ~100°C upper Triassic) and an east-to-west heating gradient.
steps.quote: maximum temperatures ranged from 110 to 140°C

steps.action: Exclude Cenozoic burial as the cause of the thermal peak, using the I/S discontinuity at the unconformity, inverse models, partially reset ZHe ages and Ro ~1.1%.
steps.quote: I/S and %Ro data together suggest that the maximum thermal peak is not related to Cenozoic sedimentation.

steps.action: Set the Triassic heating against regional thermochronology and basalt geochemistry (Enkelmann 2014; Ortíz 2021; López 2020; Martina 2021) and find them consistent.
steps.quote: Regional thermochronological data supports an interpretation of a main Triassic heating event.

steps.action: Exclude Triassic burial under a normal gradient, since it would need at least ~1500 m of unroofing that the paraconformable unconformity and regional thicknesses do not support.
steps.quote: it is unlikely that maximum temperatures were reached due to burial within a normal thermal regime.

steps.action: Estimate a Triassic gradient of 40–50°C/km from the ~70°C modelled difference over 1.3 km (plus 30% compaction) in the southern profile.
steps.quote: a geothermal gradient of 40–50°C is obtained

steps.action: Explain the west-to-east thermal asymmetry by asymmetric half-graben subsidence, complemented by the master normal fault acting as the main heat source.
steps.quote: the main heat source would have been the principal normal fault of the half-graben

steps.action: Attribute the missing Cenozoic resetting despite ~7 km of burial, and the 7–9 Ma cooling during ongoing sedimentation, to lithospheric refrigeration under flat-slab subduction, while not ruling out exhumation.
steps.quote: cooling of the involved units could be associated with the variation in the thermal flux in the region

steps.action: Build a 1D PetroMod burial and thermal model and tune the heat-flow history (90 to 70 mW/m2 in the Triassic rift, down to ~20 mW/m2 after 11 Ma) to match the peak temperatures.
steps.quote: An integrated 1D model (Figures 10, SM4a,b) was carried out in order to estimate the heat flow

steps.action: Use the PetroMod trajectories of four horizons as HeFTy forward models that predict AFT, AHe and ZHe ages for 22 and 20 mW/m2 over the last 10 Myr.
steps.quote: we carry out forward thermal models in the software HeFTy, which allow predicting thermochronological ages

steps.action: Compare predicted with observed ages: the pattern of reset versus unreset ages is reproduced for all samples except N148.
steps.quote: The predicted ages for both forward models adequately reproduce the observed pattern of reset vs unreset ages for all but sample N148

steps.action: Attribute the N148 mismatch to a known overprediction of AHe ages for high-eU grains in the Flowers et al. (2009) radiation-damage model, leaving the thermal history unchanged.
steps.quote: We attribute this pattern to the overprediction of AHe ages for high eU samples

steps.action: Keep the Triassic thermal peak and the PetroMod boundary conditions as validated.
steps.quote: reinforce our interpretation of a main thermal peak during the Triassic

steps.action: Extend the thermal model to the Triassic depocentres overlapped by the flat slab, as opposed to the Cuyana Basin model, and draw implications for hydrocarbon exploration.
steps.quote: this thermal model could be considered for these basins as opposed to the model for the southern Cuyana Basin

steps.action: Conclude that the thermal signals are decoupled from peak burial and thrust exhumation and respond to changes in basal heat flow.
steps.quote: Thermal signatures in the Ischigualasto-Villa Unión basin are decoupled from subsidence and exhumation signals

No; inferred from palaeothermometers and thermochronometers
Cenozoic foreland burial vs Mesozoic rift high heat flow
Yes: I/S discontinuity at the unconformity and unreset Triassic AFT versus continuous burial trend

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Three sections plus regional basins and published samples
Partly: constrained vs unconstrained models, two heat flows, concordance with published ages
Triassic peak kept as best explanation; Cenozoic burial excluded as peak cause; cooling mechanism not decided

end.claim: Contrary to the earlier burial model, the thermal peak occurred in the Triassic (heat flow up to ~90 mW m−2, <2 km burial, ~160°C at the base), not during the 5–7 km Cenozoic burial; Cenozoic reheating was weaker under a low gradient, and cooling began ~10–8 Ma, before thrusting.

decisive_move.sentence: Excluding Cenozoic burial as the cause of the peak, from the I/S discontinuity across the Triassic–Cretaceous unconformity combined with Ro and the inverse thermochronological models, is what makes the claim.

gates.evidence: Action: the rival hypotheses are stated in the introduction (p. 1985) and the sampling targets the age of the thermal peak (p. 1987), but the sections are described as representative rather than chosen to discriminate between the rivals. Claim: the burial hypothesis could have been supported by a continuous I/S trend or by Cenozoic resetting of Triassic AFT, and it was not (pp. 2003, 2005). However, the preferred multi-sample models impose a Triassic heating constraint (p. 2002). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

252Cf fission-fragment irradiation and the external detector method for fission tracks
Isotope-dilution He measurement by quadrupole mass spectrometry and U-Th-Sm by ICP-MS
ASTM D2797 and D7708 procedures for vitrinite reflectance

novelty_claims.quote: Despite up to 5km-thick Cenozoic overburden and unlike previously thought, the thermal peak in the basin is not due to Cenozoic burial
Decoupling between the initial signals of cooling and exhumation is seldom documented.
Our study places time and temperature constraints on flat-slab cooling
We present new coal petrography and vitrinite reflectance data

limits: Coded from the published PDF only. A peer-review history exists (publons, p. 2008) but was not supplied, so there is no review sequence. The preferred multi-sample models impose a Triassic heating constraint (p. 2002), which partly builds the conclusion into the inversion. The unconstrained runs also show a Mesozoic peak but are judged unreliable. Heat-flow values are inconsistent across the paper: the abstract gives 90, the highlights 100, and the conclusions 100/80 mW/m2, while Figure 10 shows 90/70 mW/m2 (inference: reporting error). Sample counts differ between sections: nine AFT samples (p. 1993) versus eight plus six sandstone layers (p. 1995). The chi-square test is cited to a neurosurgery paper (Galbraith & Teasdale 1981), a citation error. S-172 has only 2 track lengths. Sub-claims at different statuses: the Triassic gradient of 40–50°C/km, the Miocene heat flow below 30 mW/m2 and the cooling onset at 7–9 Ma are estimate_with_resolution with partly unstated uncertainty. Flat-slab refrigeration as the cooling mechanism is best_explanation at most, since exhumation 'cannot be ruled out' (pp. 2006, 2007). The fault-as-heat-source explanation of the asymmetry is untested. No sampling plan or analysis choices were fixed before the data. The supplementary material was not supplied, so the checks reported there (SM3, Table S3) cannot be verified.

disagreements.target: Previous hypothesis that maximum temperatures in this depocentre and neighbouring basins occurred during Cenozoic Andean burial
disagreements.support: Two distinct thermal episodes are resolved, and the Cenozoic one is weaker under a low gradient.
disagreements.quote: This contrasts with the previous hypothesis for this depocentre and for neighbouring basins

disagreements.target: Common practice in sub-Andean thermochronology of equating peak heating with peak burial and cooling onset with thrust exhumation
disagreements.support: Cooling began at 7–9 Ma during ongoing sedimentation, before thrusting at ~6 Ma or later as dated from cross-cutting relationships.
disagreements.quote: as it is commonly done in thermochronologic studies in [...]

disagreements.support: The model overpredicts AHe ages for high-eU grains, following Willett et al. (2017), which explains the N148 forward-model mismatch.

alternatives_considered.reason: The expected model lies between the more complex maximum-likelihood and the less complex maximum-posterior models

alternatives_considered.chosen: Multi-sample models with Triassic–early Jurassic residence constraint (up to 200°C, 210–180 Ma)
alternatives_considered.reason: The unconstrained models give incoherent histories for sites 35 km apart; the constraint is motivated by individual models, Triassic basalts and regional studies, and it improves the southern log-likelihood

alternatives_considered.chosen: Discordant AFT ages of Pennsylvanian samples interpreted as fully reset
alternatives_considered.reason: No correlation of ages with Dpar

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both 22 and 20 mW/m2 for the last 10 Myr
Asymmetric subsidence complemented by the master fault as heat source
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Asymmetric subsidence alone; principal normal fault as main heat source
alternatives_considered.reason: Bimodal volcanism in the Triassic column and the Makhous & Galushkin (2005) conductive model

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Burial with decreasing heat flow; thermal blanketing by cold sediments
alternatives_considered.reason: Either is required to explain the diverging t–T paths

alternatives_considered.chosen: Lithospheric refrigeration from flat-slab subduction as main cooling mechanism
alternatives_considered.reason: Cooling onset is contemporary with Mio-Pliocene sedimentation, but exhumation is not ruled out
